TSMC will begin retrofitting the plants it bought from AUO for advanced packaging as early as the 2nd quarter next year as it speeds construction work to meet massive AI-related packaging demand, media report, citing construction firms. TSMC bought 2 plants from AUO last week for NT$38.8 billion (US$1.25 billion) bring total such purchases to NT$55.94B (including NT$17.14B plant from Innolux) this year. 

The plants are also seen as part of TSMC’s strategy for next generation CoPoS advanced packaging because of the use of display-panel related equipment and expertise (both AUO and Innolux make display panels). The report notes AUO is setting up a 510x515mm glass substrate pilot line focused on TGV and RDL technologies with Corning in a bid to join TSMC’s supply chain. It also says Nvidia is testing glass-core substrates, with Innolux drilling the glass vias. 
CoPoS: Chip on Panel on Substrate
TGV: Through-Glass Via

The Mysterious Green Stone That Watched 4,000 Years of History

In the middle of a circular ring of ancient stones lies a single polished green block—silent, smooth, and strangely powerful. At first glance it may look like just another rock, but archaeologists believe this stone could be a ritual altar dating back nearly 4,000 years, to the early Bronze Age between 2500 and 2000 BCE.

Unlike the rough stones that surround it, this block is carefully shaped and polished. Its smooth surface suggests that human hands intentionally crafted it, giving it a special purpose. The stone’s striking green color hints that it may be made from serpentine or a jade-like mineral, materials that many ancient cultures associated with fertility, renewal, and spiritual power.

But the most fascinating detail is its position. The stone sits at the very center of a circular enclosure, as if everything around it was built to focus attention on this single object. Imagine a time thousands of years ago, when people gathered here under the open sky. Fires flickered, voices whispered prayers, and rituals may have taken place around this very stone.

Was it used for offerings to unknown gods? Did it mark a sacred meeting place for an ancient community? Or did it represent something even deeper—an attempt by early humans to connect with the forces of nature surrounding them?

Today, the green stone remains quiet and unmoving, yet it continues to spark curiosity. After four millennia, it still invites us to wonder about the beliefs, fears, and hopes of the people who once stood around it, staring into the same sky we see today.

Some stones are just stones.
But others are fragments of forgotten worlds.
